body:
Understanding the contribution of national leaders

The Indian National Movement was not the achievement of one person or one organisation. Political leaders, social reformers, writers, educationists, revolutionaries and community organisers contributed in different ways to the struggle against colonial rule. Their methods sometimes differed, but their activities helped Indians develop political awareness, demand rights and work towards freedom.

The Indian National Congress (INC), established at Bombay in 1885, provided an important platform for organised political activity. Its early leaders mainly used constitutional methods. Later leaders encouraged wider public participation through swadeshi, boycott, satyagraha and other forms of resistance.

What does field-wise contribution mean?

A leader's field of contribution is the principal area in which that person influenced the national movement. For example, Dadabhai Naoroji explained the economic consequences of colonial rule, Bal Gangadhar Tilak popularised assertive nationalism, and B. R. Ambedkar fought for social equality and political representation.

Some leaders worked in more than one field. Jawaharlal Nehru was a freedom fighter and later a leader of independent India. Rabindranath Tagore contributed through literature, education and criticism of colonial injustice. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel organised farmers before independence and helped integrate princely states afterwards.

Major fields of contribution

  • Economic criticism: Dadabhai Naoroji explained the drain of wealth from India under British rule.
  • Constitutional nationalism: Gopal Krishna Gokhale advocated political reforms through legislative discussion, persuasion and public service.
  • Assertive nationalism: Bal Gangadhar Tilak emphasised swaraj, swadeshi, boycott and popular mobilisation.
  • Non-violent mass struggle: Mahatma Gandhi organised satyagrahas and nationwide campaigns against British rule.
  • Social justice: B. R. Ambedkar fought untouchability and demanded equal rights and political safeguards.
  • Armed anti-colonial struggle: Subhas Chandra Bose led the reorganised Indian National Army.
  • Political leadership and national integration: Jawaharlal Nehru and Vallabhbhai Patel played major roles in the transition to independence.
  • Cultural and educational awakening: Rabindranath Tagore strengthened cultural confidence and promoted a broad humanistic outlook.
  • Non-violent community organisation: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan organised the Khudai Khidmatgars in the North-West Frontier Province.
  • Post-independence constructive reform: Vinoba Bhave promoted voluntary land redistribution through the Bhoodan Movement.

How to distinguish their methods

Constitutional nationalism relied mainly on petitions, public meetings, legislative debate and demands for reform. Assertive nationalism placed greater emphasis on self-reliance, boycott and public pressure. Satyagraha used non-violent resistance to challenge injustice. Revolutionary nationalism included organisations that considered armed struggle necessary to end colonial rule.

These distinctions should not be treated as completely separate political organisations or fixed personal identities. Leaders could agree on the objective of freedom while disagreeing about the best method of achieving it.

Prelims focus

  • The Indian National Congress was established at Bombay in 1885.
  • Naoroji is associated with economic criticism of British rule.
  • Gokhale represents moderate constitutional nationalism.
  • Tilak is associated with assertive nationalism and swaraj.
  • Ambedkar's central contribution includes social justice and constitutional safeguards.
  • Trap: Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan Movement began after independence, not during the main anti-colonial struggle.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 109–115; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Chapter 3, Nationalism in India, printed pp. 53–55.]

body:
The early constitutional approach

During its early decades, the Indian National Congress demanded greater Indian participation in administration, representative institutions, civil service reform and fairer economic policies. Many of its leaders believed that informed public opinion and constitutional pressure could persuade the British government to introduce reforms.

Two important leaders of this phase were Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale. Both criticised colonial rule, but their most recognisable contributions were different: Naoroji explained its economic consequences, while Gokhale combined constitutional politics with education and public service.

Dadabhai Naoroji: The economic critique of colonialism

Drain of Wealth Theory

Dadabhai Naoroji, widely known as the Grand Old Man of India, argued that British rule caused a continuing transfer of Indian resources to Britain without an equivalent economic return to India. This became known as the Drain of Wealth Theory.

The drain included payments connected with British administration, pensions, salaries and other remittances abroad. Naoroji argued that such transfers reduced the resources available for India's economic development and contributed to poverty.

Drain of wealth: A transfer of resources or income from India to Britain without an equivalent return benefiting the Indian economy.

Naoroji systematically explained this argument in his book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, published in 1901. The significance of the argument was political as well as economic: it challenged the claim that colonial rule was necessarily beneficial to Indians.

Institutions and important years

  • 1866: Naoroji established the East India Association in London to present Indian concerns to British audiences.
  • 1886: He presided over the Indian National Congress session at Calcutta.
  • 1892: He was elected to the British House of Commons from Finsbury Central, London.
  • 1901: His book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India appeared.
  • 1906: He presided over the Calcutta Congress session, where swaraj or self-government became a central political demand.

Gopal Krishna Gokhale: Reform through public service

Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a leading Moderate nationalist. He believed in constitutional methods, legislative discussion, reasoned criticism of government policy and the gradual expansion of Indian self-government.

Gokhale attached particular importance to education. He believed that wider education would strengthen political awareness and enable Indians to participate more effectively in public affairs. He advocated the expansion of primary education and criticised social inequalities.

In 1905, Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society at Pune. Its purpose was to train people for dedicated public service and the advancement of national interests through constitutional methods. He also presided over the 1905 Benares Congress session.

Gokhale influenced Mahatma Gandhi's understanding of Indian political and social conditions. Gandhi regarded him as an important political guide.

Naoroji and Gokhale compared

AspectDadabhai NaorojiGopal Krishna Gokhale
Principal fieldEconomic nationalismConstitutional reform and public service
Key ideaDrain of wealthGradual political reform and education
Major institutionEast India Association, 1866Servants of India Society, 1905
Important workPoverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901Legislative advocacy and public education
Congress associationCalcutta session, 1906Benares session, 1905

Both leaders opposed colonial injustice, but they should not be confused with revolutionaries advocating an armed overthrow of British rule. Their approach helped establish the economic and political arguments on which later mass nationalism developed.

Prelims focus

  • Dadabhai Naoroji: Drain of Wealth Theory.
  • East India Association: London, 1866.
  • Naoroji entered the British House of Commons in 1892.
  • Gokhale founded the Servants of India Society in 1905.
  • Gokhale presided over the Benares Congress session in 1905.
  • Trap: The Servants of India Society was founded by Gokhale, not Naoroji.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 111–112; Indian National Congress, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Past Party Presidents, section on the Servants of India Society; Indian National Congress, Dadabhai Naoroji: Pioneer of Indian Nationalism, sections on the British Parliament and the 1906 Congress session; UK Parliament Heritage Collections, Dadabhai Naoroji, 1892–1895. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

body:
Bal Gangadhar Tilak and assertive nationalism

Bal Gangadhar Tilak, popularly known as Lokmanya Tilak, was a prominent advocate of assertive nationalism. He believed that Indians should actively demand self-government rather than depend mainly on petitions and appeals to British goodwill.

Tilak popularised the demand for swaraj, meaning self-government or self-rule. He is closely associated with the declaration that freedom was his birthright. His politics emphasised political awakening, self-reliance and wider public participation.

Newspapers and public awareness

Tilak used newspapers to criticise colonial policies and spread nationalist ideas. Two publications strongly associated with him were Kesari, published in Marathi, and The Mahratta, published in English.

He also helped make public celebrations of Ganapati and Shivaji important occasions for political mobilisation in Maharashtra. These activities brought nationalist discussion beyond the limited circle of educated political associations.

Swadeshi and the response to Bengal's partition

In 1905, the British government under Viceroy Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal. Opposition to the partition helped generate the Swadeshi Movement.

Swadeshi meant supporting goods produced in India and encouraging Indian enterprise. Boycott meant refusing to buy foreign goods or participate in selected colonial institutions as an act of protest. Nationalists also encouraged national education and the use of Indian languages.

The movement was especially strong in Bengal but influenced political activity elsewhere. Tilak was one of the leaders who supported assertive methods of struggle.

Lal-Bal-Pal

The expression Lal-Bal-Pal refers to three prominent assertive nationalists:

  • Lal: Lala Lajpat Rai, associated particularly with Punjab.
  • Bal: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, associated with Maharashtra.
  • Pal: Bipin Chandra Pal, associated with Bengal.

These leaders supported stronger public mobilisation and criticised the limitations of moderate political methods. Their approaches were not identical, but they are grouped together because of their role in developing assertive nationalism.

The Surat Split of 1907

Differences between Moderates and assertive nationalists intensified over political objectives and methods, including boycott. At the Surat session of the Congress in 1907, these disagreements resulted in a split.

Surat, in present-day Gujarat, is therefore an important place in the political history of the national movement. The dispute was within the Congress; it should not be confused with the partition of Bengal in 1905.

Home Rule Leagues in 1916

The Home Rule Movement demanded self-government for India. In 1916, Tilak and Annie Besant organised separate but related Home Rule Leagues to popularise this demand.

  • Bal Gangadhar Tilak: Established his Home Rule League in April 1916, with an important base in western India.
  • Annie Besant: Launched her Home Rule League in September 1916 and used publications such as New India to promote self-government.

Home Rule was a demand for self-government and organised political pressure. It was not the name of an armed revolutionary organisation. The movement helped revive political mobilisation during the First World War.

In 1917, Annie Besant became the first woman President of the Indian National Congress, presiding over its Calcutta session.

Prelims focus

  • Tilak: Kesari in Marathi and The Mahratta in English.
  • Lal-Bal-Pal: Lajpat Rai, Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
  • Partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi Movement: 1905.
  • Surat Split of the Congress: 1907.
  • Tilak and Annie Besant organised separate Home Rule Leagues in 1916.
  • Trap: Annie Besant was the first woman Congress President in 1917; Sarojini Naidu was the first Indian woman Congress President in 1925.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 112–114; Indian National Congress, Annie Besant, Past Party Presidents, sections on Home Rule and the 1917 presidency; Indian National Congress, Tilak: The Revolutionary Nationalist, section on the Home Rule Movement; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, Benares 1905 and Surat 1907 sessions. Online sources consulted 22 November 2026.]

body:
Gandhi's principal field of contribution

Mahatma Gandhi transformed the Indian National Movement by involving large sections of society in organised political resistance. Farmers, workers, students, women and other groups participated in movements that linked the demand for independence with everyday grievances.

Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in January 1915. His experience of opposing racial discrimination through non-violent resistance influenced his subsequent campaigns in India.

The meaning of satyagraha

Satyagraha is a method of resistance based on truth, non-violence and the willingness to endure suffering rather than inflict it on an opponent.

For Gandhi, satyagraha was not passive acceptance of injustice. It required active resistance, discipline and a willingness to accept the consequences of peaceful protest.

Two related methods must be distinguished. Non-cooperation involved withdrawing support from colonial institutions and activities. Civil disobedience involved deliberately and non-violently breaking an unjust law. Both could be part of the wider practice of satyagraha.

Early satyagrahas and local grievances

Champaran, Bihar: 1917

Gandhi intervened in the grievances of indigo cultivators subjected to an oppressive plantation system. Champaran became an important example of how local agrarian problems could be challenged through organised non-violent action.

Kheda, Gujarat: 1918

Farmers in Kheda faced difficulties in paying land revenue after agricultural distress. Gandhi supported their demand for relief from revenue collection. Vallabhbhai Patel was an important organiser of the campaign.

Ahmedabad, Gujarat: 1918

Gandhi became involved in a dispute concerning textile mill workers. The Ahmedabad movement demonstrated the application of satyagraha to an industrial labour dispute rather than an agricultural question.

Major nationwide movements

  • Rowlatt Satyagraha, 1919: Gandhi called for nationwide peaceful opposition to the Rowlatt Act, which strengthened repressive powers and permitted detention without trial.
  • Non-Cooperation Movement, 1920–1922: Protesters boycotted government-controlled institutions, surrendered titles and rejected foreign goods. Gandhi withdrew the movement after the violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922.
  • Civil Disobedience Movement, 1930: Gandhi challenged the salt law by marching to Dandi in Gujarat and breaking the law on 6 April 1930.
  • Quit India Movement, 1942: Gandhi called for an immediate end to British rule during the Second World War. The movement became associated with the expression Do or Die.

Why the Dandi March mattered

Salt was essential to every household. By challenging the government's monopoly and tax on salt, Gandhi selected an issue that affected people across income groups. The march began at Sabarmati Ashram and ended at Dandi on the Gujarat coast, where the salt law was broken on 6 April 1930.

The movement demonstrated how a familiar economic burden could become a symbol of national resistance. It also gave Gujarat a particularly important place in the history of civil disobedience.

Gandhi's connection with other national leaders

Gandhi's movements involved collaboration and disagreement. Patel helped organise farmers in Gujarat. Nehru became a major Congress leader during the phase of mass nationalism. Ambedkar agreed that untouchability was unjust but differed with Gandhi over political representation for the Depressed Classes. Subhas Chandra Bose respected Gandhi's national leadership while disagreeing with non-violence as the exclusive method of achieving independence.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhi returned to India in January 1915.
  • Champaran: indigo cultivators, Bihar, 1917.
  • Kheda: land revenue relief, Gujarat, 1918.
  • Ahmedabad: textile mill workers, 1918.
  • Dandi: Salt Satyagraha, 6 April 1930.
  • Trap: The Non-Cooperation Movement was withdrawn in 1922 after Chauri Chaura; the Salt Satyagraha began in 1930.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, Chapter 3, Nationalism in India, sections The Idea of Satyagraha, The Rowlatt Act and Towards Civil Disobedience, printed pp. 54–64; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 9, printed pp. 115–124; Indian National Congress, Brief History of Congress, 1915–1925, entry on the Kheda Satyagraha. Online source consulted 22 November 2026.]
